\chapter{Communication Complexity — Func Disjointness}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.FuncDisjointness
\section{Overview}

This module establishes the exact deterministic communication complexity of the
set-disjointness function on subsets of $[n]$.  Using a fooling-set argument based on
the pairs $(X, X^c)$, it shows that for $n \ge 1$ the complexity is exactly $n + 1$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Set disjointness function]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\leanok
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and subsets $X, Y \subseteq [n]$, $\mathrm{disjointness}(n, X, Y)$
is the Boolean function that returns $\mathtt{true}$ if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are
disjoint, i.e.\ $X \cap Y = \emptyset$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Commutativity of disjointness]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness_comm}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness_comm}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\difficulty{2}
The disjointness function is symmetric in its two set arguments: for all
$X, Y \subseteq [n]$, $\mathrm{disjointness}(n, X, Y) = \mathrm{disjointness}(n, Y, X)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Fooling set for disjointness]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet}
\leanok
The candidate fooling set for disjointness is the collection of all pairs
$(X, X^c)$ where $X \subseteq [n]$, i.e.\ $\mathrm{foolingSet}(n) = \{(X, Y) \mid Y = X^c\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fooling set validity]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet_isFoolingSet}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet_isFoolingSet}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.IsFoolingSet, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.IsRectangle_iff}
\difficulty{5}
The collection $\{(X, X^c) \mid X \subseteq [n]\}$ is a fooling set for
$\mathrm{disjointness}(n)$: every pair $(X, X^c)$ evaluates to $\mathtt{true}$,
and for any monochromatic rectangle $R$ with $\mathrm{disjointness} = \mathtt{true}$
that contains two distinct fooling-set pairs, those pairs must coincide.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fooling set cardinality]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet_card}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet_card}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet}
\difficulty{4}
The fooling set $\mathrm{foolingSet}(n)$ has cardinality $2^n$, since it is in
bijection with the power set of $[n]$ via $X \mapsto (X, X^c)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound on complexity of disjointness]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.communicationComplexity_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.communicationComplexity_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity_le_clog_card_X_alpha, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\difficulty{3}
The deterministic communication complexity of $\mathrm{disjointness}(n)$ is at most
$n + 1$: Alice can communicate her entire set $X \subseteq [n]$ in $n$ bits, after
which Bob sends a single bit for the answer.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound on complexity of disjointness]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.le_communicationComplexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.le_communicationComplexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.le_communicationComplexity_of_forall_lt_ncard, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet_isFoolingSet, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_point_mem, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_values_eq}
\difficulty{6}
For $n \ge 1$, the deterministic communication complexity of $\mathrm{disjointness}(n)$
is at least $n + 1$.  The proof uses the fooling set of size $2^n$ together with an
additional input $(x_0, y_0)$ with $x_0 \cap y_0 \ne \emptyset$ to show that any
monochromatic partition of the input space into rectangles requires more than $2^n$
pieces.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact complexity of disjointness]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.communicationComplexity_eq}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.communicationComplexity_eq}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.communicationComplexity_le, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.le_communicationComplexity}
\difficulty{1}
For $n \ge 1$, the deterministic communication complexity of the set-disjointness
function on subsets of $[n]$ is exactly $n + 1$.  This follows by combining the
matching upper and lower bounds.
\end{theorem}
